lesson.title: Twin Suppletions
lesson.subtitle: gut/besser/hoch/höher vs good/better/high/higher — the shared irregular story

hook.title: Irregular Together
hook.content: Suppletion — replacing a missing form with a borrowed word — is the rarest grammar event, and English and German did the SAME rare events on the SAME verbs. good/better ↔ gut/besser: both replaced their comparative with a form of *bazizon. much/more ↔ viel/mehr: both borrowed *maizô. high/higher stayed native in both — hoch/höher with pure umlaut. The odds of coincidence are zero: these pairs were irregular together before the languages split, and both kept the irregulars because irregulars are frequency armor — the most-used words resist regularization longest.

footnotes.title: Why Irregulars Survive
footnotes.content: Regular verbs and adjectives regularize when they are rare — nobody says 'goed' for the verb they use hourly. Irregularity is protection by usage: the top-100 words keep their ancient forms because everyone hears them a thousand times a day. That is why the suppletive twins survived on BOTH shores.

pattern.title: The Twin Pairs, Filed
pattern.content: Pair one: gut → besser ↔ good → better — the *bazizon loan, shifted per the laws (b stays, ss/tz reports T→SS/Z). Pair two: viel → mehr ↔ much → more — *maizô, with mehr's r intact. Pair three: hoch → höher ↔ high → higher — the gh→ch word with pure umlaut, no borrowing needed. Pair four — the failed pair: gut → best ↔ good → best (identical superlative!), and am besten ↔ the best. Also file: viel → am meisten ↔ the most (meist/most — another twin hiding in the superlative). Two borrowings, one umlaut, four twin pairs — the irregular hall is shared property.
pattern.linguist_note: besser's ss and better's tt both encode the same dental: T→SS/Z on the German side, and English's own old tt. The comparative was borrowed BEFORE the High German shift — so the shift applied to it like a native. Borrowed-then-shifted: the signature of ancient loans.

exercises.prompt: The twin pairs — match the irregulars:
exercises.explanation: Two borrowed comparatives and one umlaut native — all shared across the sea.

exercises.prompt: Why are gut/besser and good/better BOTH irregular?
options: Both replaced their comparative with the same ancient word (*bazizon) before they split
exercises.target_answer: Both replaced their comparative with the same ancient word (*bazizon) before they split
exercises.explanation: The borrowing happened in Proto-Germanic — both languages inherited the irregularity, then shifted it independently.

exercises.prompt: Which superlative twin hides in 'am meisten' (the most)?
exercises.meaning: viel → am meisten ↔ much → the most
exercises.explanation: meist and most are the same superlative — the mehr/more twin continues one rung up the ladder.

exercises.prompt: Answer the question using the comparative:
exercises.reply_idea: Reply: Yes, it is colder today.
cues: Add heute and the umlauted comparative kälter.
exercises.explanation: Short Germanic adjectives like kalt raise their vowel with an umlaut in the comparative: kalt → kälter.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'The book is better, but the film is the best':
exercises.target_answer: Das Buch ist besser aber der Film ist am besten
exercises.meaning: The book is better, but the film is the best

vocab_hints.note: der Film — a direct loan, identical word

exercises.explanation: besser (the *bazizon twin) and am besten (the best twin) in one verdict — the suppletion ladder complete.

summary.outcome: Use besser, mehr, höher, am besten — and explain each as shared inheritance.

use_example.german: Das Buch ist besser, aber der Film ist am besten.
use_example.english: The book is better, but the film is the best.

summary.takeaway: Suppletion is shared: gut/besser ↔ good/better, viel/mehr ↔ much/more — irregular together, irregular forever.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the -er/-ste Sentence Gym — twenty comparison sentences with als and wie.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "Today that is very good"
twist.explanation: Building "Heute ist das sehr gut" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Twin Suppletions.

hoch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hauhaz — the twin of high, with high's gh still sounding as the Ach-Laut ch. Comparative: höher (high→higher). [wiktionary]

mehr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *maizô — the twin of more (and its cousin most/meist); the r survived, the vowel lengthened. [wiktionary]

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

schwager.context_phrase: Mein Schwager arbeitet bei einer Bank.
schwager.context_translation: My brother-in-law works at a bank.
schwager.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *swāgr 'husband's brother'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

baby.context_translation: The baby is sleeping in the nursery.
baby.etymology_derivation: Mid-19th-century borrowing from English baby — a loan, not an inherited cognate. [wiktionary]

kopf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kuppaz 'round object'; originally a drinking vessel — cognate with archaic English cop. [wiktionary]

ja.context_translation: Yes, I am happy to come along.
ja.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ja; the German section names only Yiddish — the yea link is not on the page. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

senf.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic senap, an early borrowing of Latin sinapis, itself from Greek; English keeps the same word only in technical sinap terms and uses mustard instead. [wiktionary]

frei.etymology_derivation: From Old High German frī, Proto-West Germanic *frī, the exact twin of English free; both go back to the Indo-European root meaning beloved, the same root that gave German Freund and English friend. [wiktionary]

baumwolle.context_phrase: Dieses Hemd ist aus reiner Baumwolle.
baumwolle.context_translation: This shirt is made of pure cotton.
baumwolle.etymology_derivation: Baum (tree) + Wolle (wool): cotton, literally tree-wool - a name going back to Herodotus's tale of wool-bearing trees. [wiktionary]

telefonnummer.context_translation: I write down my phone number.
telefonnummer.etymology_derivation: Telefon plus Nummer (number — Latin numerus, the same word behind English number); Telefon is the same Greek-built international word as telephone. [wiktionary]

summe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin summa, the total - English sum is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]
